newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition, SPD strike tax bill compromise. [CORRECTED 17:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: German coalition, SPD strike tax bill compromise. [CORRECTED 17:55 GMT]

text.p: Germany's coalition government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have struck a compromise to open the way for the 1997 tax bill to pass, negotiators said before (corrects from after) parliament's mediation committee met on Thursday.
The deal means that the last element of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to get German state finances into shape for European monetary union should fall into place.
The SPD, which has a blocking majority in the upper house of parliament, had been fighting to keep a wealth tax which had been ruled illegal by the constitutional court.
But the party caved in last week after the government threatened to let the bill fail -- which would have meant that the tax would have been abolished automatically next year.
The two sides agreed to tax changes which would help raise an extra 8.2 billion marks in revenues for Germany's 16 states to compensate for the loss in wealth tax revenues.

Increases in inheritance taxes and a bigger-than-planned rise in property dealing tax to 3.5 percent from two percent will raise the extra revenues. Losses from abolishing the wealth tax had been estimated at 9.3 billion marks.
The SPD still wants to keep the tax on private fortunes, but party officials said they would not block the tax bill on that score. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
